overview.headline: Continuous circulation of water between ground and atmosphere

keyPoints.point: Students learn that continuous circulation moves water through the Earth-Atmosphere system in the hydrologic cycle.
keyPoints.quote: The hydrologic cycle involves the continuous circulation of water in the Earth-Atmosphere system.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that energy is required for evaporation to take place from liquid water.
keyPoints.quote: For evaporation to take place, energy is required.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that foggy conditions occur when air temperature equals the dew point temperature.
keyPoints.quote: Foggy conditions often occur when air temperature and dew point are equal.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that runoff occurs when excessive precipitation leaves the ground saturated and unable to absorb more water.
keyPoints.quote: Runoff occurs when there is excessive precipitation and the ground is saturated (cannot absorb any more water).

keyTerms.gloss: Change from liquid to gas that requires energy input
keyTerms.quote: For evaporation to take place, energy is required.

keyTerms.gloss: Passive loss of water vapor from plants controlled by humidity
keyTerms.quote: In most plants, transpiration is a passive process largely controlled by the humidity of the atmosphere and the moisture content of the soil.

keyTerms.gloss: Change from vapor to liquid that may appear as clouds or dew
keyTerms.quote: In the atmosphere, condensation may appear as clouds or dew.

keyTerms.gloss: Water falling to Earth when precipitation particles grow too large to stay aloft
keyTerms.quote: Runoff occurs when there is excessive precipitation and the ground is saturated (cannot absorb any more water).

keyTerms.gloss: Excess water that forms rivers and lakes when ground cannot absorb more
keyTerms.quote: Rivers and lakes are results of runoff.
